finding: §3's canonical illustration of the change rule is impossible under the precedence §2 states, and it contradicts a sentence three lines above it. §3: "a `--project` write of `all` that *uncovers* a task override of `blocking` changes the resolved value and must be refused." Under §2's precedence — task override > project config > built-in, pinned by §7 test 2 and implemented in engine/configresolve.go ResolveWorkflowLayers, which reads the task override first for every field — a task override of `blocking` is never covered by anything: it already wins before the write and still wins after it. Resolved-before equals resolved-after, so by §3's own rule that write must PASS. The project layer is the lower one; a project write cannot uncover a task override, only the reverse (removing a task override of `all` uncovers a project `blocking`, and that is a deletion, not a write of `all`). The paragraph is also falsified in the other direction by §3 line 156-157: "a write of `all` never trips it, since `all` is the default and the only value that tightens the gate". §7 test 13 takes that second side ("the writes that must **pass**: any write of `all`"), so whichever reading is intended, one of §3 and §7 is wrong and an implementer cannot tell which.
suggestion: Delete the uncover clause or restate it in the only direction the precedence admits: a write or removal at the TASK layer that uncovers a project-layer `blocking` changes the resolved value and is refused. Then reconcile 'a write of `all` never trips it' with whichever cases survive, and make §7 test 13 name the surviving set rather than 'any write of `all`'.

finding: §4's emission predicate, added this round, makes the two buckets §4 exists to protect identically zero on every payload that carries the key. Emission: "when the merged round would be clean under the resolved policy *and* holds at least one non-`PASS` row". Buckets: "`error` + `unrecognised` sums the round's blocking rows and the two sections cannot drift apart." By §2's predicate a round is clean under `blocking` exactly when no non-`PASS` row carries a blocking severity, and §2 makes an unrecognised severity blocking — so on every emitted `by_severity`, `error` = 0 and `unrecognised` = 0 by construction; under `all` the key is never emitted at all. The sum §4 names is therefore always 0 = 0. Consequences: (a) 'Every row lands in a named bucket, because the point is that nothing hides' is true only of `warning` and `info`, the two that never hid; (b) '`""` is not a bucket … it is the hiding this section exists to prevent' guards a population that cannot appear; (c) §7 test 17 ('`error` + `unrecognised` equals the round's blocking-row count over a fixture carrying all four unrecognised shapes') cannot be written against an emitted payload, and its named killing input — 'a `""` bucket, or splitting the four' — does not kill, because every bucketing rule agrees on an empty population.
suggestion: Decide which §4 wants. Either emit `by_severity` on every round holding a non-`PASS` row (so `error`/`unrecognised` are reachable and the sum is checkable, at the cost of the presence signal §4 argues for), or keep the clean-only condition and drop the `error`/`unrecognised` reachability argument and test 17 with it, stating instead that an emitted breakdown holds only advisory severities by construction.

finding: §4 gates emission on a workflow field at a sink that has no spec context and, by shipped design, refuses one — so 'resolves the same field `--record` will' cannot hold. §4: "`--merge` can evaluate that condition — it holds the round's rows and resolves the same field `--record` will." Measured: `engine.ResolveWorkflow(specPath, explicitFile)` (internal/engine/workflow_resolve.go:16-36) reaches the task-override layer only through `specMatches(tfPath, tf.Spec, specPath)` or `SpecAdjacentTaskFile(specPath)`; with no spec path both branches fall through and resolution degrades to project config > built-in, dropping the top layer of the precedence §2 states and §7 test 2 pins. `runAuditMerge` (internal/cli/audit_merge.go:19-46) takes only NDJSON inputs and rejects a spec-looking positional at entry with exit 2, while `--record` resolves against the spec named on ITS command line (audit_record.go:44, :91). The only substitute available to `--merge` is `DiscoverTaskFile(".", flagFile)` — the active pointer — which in a repository with several task files in flight (this one) resolves a DIFFERENT spec's override from the one the round belongs to, so the key would appear or vanish according to `.tp/local.json`, silently; §7 tests 15/16 pin presence without pinning whose policy decided it. REFERENCE.md:762 records that `--merge` carries no policy-aware output today, which is the invariant being changed without saying so.
suggestion: State the resolution rule for `--merge` explicitly: either give it an explicit selector (a spec or `--file`) for the policy it resolves, or specify that it resolves project config > built-in only, say so where §2 states the precedence, and add a §7 row asserting which layer `--merge` reads. Either way drop 'the same field `--record` will' unless a mechanism makes it true.

finding: §2 changes `clean` without noticing that the shipped `divergence` signal is built on the equivalence it breaks, and the inversion silences the signal exactly where `blocking` makes it decision-relevant. `engine.ComputeAuditDivergence` (internal/engine/divergence.go:95-127) emits only when five conditions hold, of which 4 is 'the sequence is not converged', and its own doc comment states the premise: "Condition 4 is redundant in every sane configuration, since condition 2 makes the latest round unclean and that is what convergence counts." Under `blocking` condition 2 (a non-`PASS` row not attributed to spec-coverage) no longer makes the round unclean — a `warning` row leaves `clean: true` — so condition 4 stops being redundant and starts SUPPRESSING the object on precisely the state the release creates: spec-coverage clean, other roles open at advisory severity, gate open. Where the sequence is not yet converged the object is emitted but `next_action` now takes the 'run the next audit round' branch instead of the fix-and-re-audit directive, falsifying REFERENCE.md:883-885 ("Whenever `divergence` is emitted over state tp itself recorded, `next_action` reads the fix-and-re-audit directive"). §2 enumerates the surfaces that stay severity-blind and `divergence` is not among them; §6's Non-Goal 1 defers only the `--check` role-scoping divergence, which is a different subject.
suggestion: Decide `divergence`'s behaviour under `blocking` in §2 beside `next_action`: either condition 4 is re-stated over the severity-blind non-`PASS` count so the object survives a clean-under-blocking round, or the release states that `divergence` is withheld once the gate opens and says why. Add it to the enumerated list of `clean` consumers, and give it a §7 row.

finding: §6a closes the reversal set at three ("The count is three because earlier drafts said one and then two"), and at least two further shipped assertions are falsified by §2 — both in the same document §6a already edits. (1) `skills/tp/REFERENCE.md:753-756`: "The audit gate is untouched: `engine.Converged`, `engine.ConsecutiveClean`, the stored per-round `clean` flag, the exit code of `tp audit --status --check`, and `next_action`'s three-state audit precedence all behave exactly as in v0.32.0." §2 changes the stored `clean` flag's meaning, changes which `next_action` branch fires and adds a fourth recommendation, and therefore changes `--status --check`'s exit code on the same rounds. (2) `internal/engine/nextaction.go:63-75` documents the same 'three-state precedence' in the constructor's own doc comment, so the count §2 makes four is pinned in code as well as docs. §6a's closing claim — "Each replacement states a rule true under **both** values of the field" — cannot be satisfied for artifacts the section does not name, and §6a's own reason for existing (a decomposer reads this list to size the coordinated edit) is what the omission defeats.
suggestion: Re-derive the reversal set by searching the shipped artifacts for assertions over `clean`, `next_action`'s branch count and `--status --check`, and state the count as whatever that search returns rather than as a corrected literal. At minimum add REFERENCE.md:753-756 and nextaction.go's 'three-state precedence' comment, and extend §7 test 19 to cover them.

finding: §2.1's convergence bound is off by one and is falsifiable as stated. "setting it at round *k* converges no earlier than *k* + `audit_clean_rounds`". `engine.Converged` is `ConsecutiveClean(rounds) >= requiredCleanRounds && !stale` and `ConsecutiveClean` is the trailing run (reviewstate.go:428-438, :509-511), so if the field resolves before round *k* is recorded and rounds *k* … *k*+cr−1 are all clean, the streak reaches cr at round *k* + cr − 1 — one round earlier than the stated floor. The table's own k=1, cr=2 cell reads 3 only because v0.35.0's round 1 was not clean under `blocking`; the bound is not tight, and a bound stated as 'no earlier than' is false when a reachable case beats it. The second paragraph's k=1, cr=1 pair (converges at 2) has the same shape.
suggestion: Either write the bound as *k* + `audit_clean_rounds` − 1, or say explicitly that *k* names the last round recorded BEFORE the knob resolves (which makes the stated formula exact) — the surrounding sentence, 'a round recorded before the knob is set keeps `clean: false` for ever', reads the other way.

finding: The derivation column added this round — §7's stated fix for a test list that lags its decisions — mis-cites in its own first use, and its framing sentence names a structure the spec does not have. Test 8's 'derives from' cell reads '§2 *unrecognised*' and its assertion enumerates four shapes: "outside the enum, `null`, absent, **or not a string** — four fixtures". §2's `unrecognised` paragraph names no shapes at all ("An unrecognised severity is treated as blocking. Not rejected, not ignored. A row tp cannot grade is a row tp must not stop counting."); the four-shape enumeration exists only in §4 ("a string outside the enum, JSON `null`, an absent key, a value that is not a string"). So the row that most needs the column points at a section that cannot move when the enumeration moves — the exact drift the column was introduced to make visible. Separately, §7's opening asserts "Every test here is derived from a **numbered** decision above", while every cell cites an italicised paragraph lead-in (§2 *Default*, §2 *The field*, §2 *stamped*, §4 *buckets*); §2's decisions carry no numbers, so 'numbered' names a scheme the document does not define.
suggestion: Point test 8 at §4 *buckets* (or move the four-shape enumeration into §2's `unrecognised` paragraph, which is where the gate rule lives, and leave §4 citing §2). Replace 'a numbered decision' with the anchor form the column actually uses, or number §2's decisions so the citation is checkable.

finding: §7's new opening attributes to round 9 a measurement round 9 did not record. "Rounds 8 and 9 both changed §2, §3 and §4 without changing this list, and round 9 measured the cost: the list went from 14 of 14 writable and 11 discriminating to 12 and 8, with four tests demanding the implementation the sections had just rejected." Counted against `spec/.tp-review/0.37.0/review-round-9.ndjson`: the strings '14 of 14', '11 discriminating', '12' and '8' as test-list counts appear nowhere; the only 'writable' figure in the round is a task-decomposability verdict ('THIRTEEN tasks, of which eleven are writable now'), a different subject and a different denominator. The round's recorded rows do flag tests 8, 9, 11, 13 and 14, which is five, not four. The claim is exactly the shape CLAUDE.md's own rule names — a quantifier over a set the author did not enumerate, in a paragraph whose whole point is that an unmaintained list is measurable — and unlike the counts in §1, §2 and §7 test 6, which all verify exactly against the corpus, this one has no artifact behind it.
suggestion: Either bind the numbers to the artifact (name the round file and the rule by which a test counts as writable/discriminating, so the figures can be re-derived) or delete the sentence and keep the decision it introduces: the derivation column exists so a changed decision with an untouched row is visible.

finding: §1 deliverable 3's replacement text is still the inverse of §4's rule, in a new way. §1: "the breakdown that makes a `blocking` round's verdict readable, emitted on the rounds where there is something to read." §4 emits it only when the round would be CLEAN under the resolved policy and holds a non-`PASS` row — so it is absent on every round whose verdict is 'not clean', which is the round where an operator asks what blocked it and the only round on which `error` and `unrecognised` are non-zero. The rounds where there is most to read are exactly the rounds with no breakdown. §1 also still presents deliverable 3 as one of three things the release buys while, by §4's own paragraph, the key is unreachable by construction for every project on the default — which §1 deliverable 1 says is every project that does not set the field.
suggestion: Restate deliverable 3 as what §4 decides: the breakdown that shows what a clean-under-`blocking` round accepted, emitted only on such a round and therefore only for projects that opt in. Do not paraphrase §4's condition in §1 at all if the two keep diverging — name the section and stop.

finding: The rewritten test table numbers its rows 1-19 but carries 20 rows, because 9b sits between 9 and 10. Every cross-reference to a test in this cycle is by number ('§7 test 11', 'test 13'), and §5/§6/§2 use the same form for cross-spec pointers, so a table whose ids are not a contiguous integer sequence makes 'test N' ambiguous between position and label, and makes a later renumber silent. §6a's own history in this file is the precedent: three earlier rounds recorded pointers to '§5 test 12' and '§5 test 9' that resolved to the wrong row after a list changed length.
suggestion: Renumber the rows 1-20 and let the derivation column carry the pairing that 9/9b was expressing (both cite §2 *stamped*), so an id is a position and a pointer cannot drift.
